Cardano (CRYPTO: ADA) is trading about 95% below its all-time high of $3.10, reached in September 2021. Cardano’s price history shows the coin has hit five earlier lows, each down 90% or more from a previous high. Investors have seen almost the entire 16,332% increase that ADA achieved from its low of 1.88 cents in March 2020 to that peak wiped out. ADA now trades around 15.4 cents.
In 2026, sellers have been particularly aggressive. Since December 31, 2025, ADA has plummeted by 56.9%, and it has fallen 30.9% over the past month, reaching an intraday low of 13.32 cents on November 21, 2026. Over the last five years, it has lost 91.4%.
Cardano isn’t alone in drops this deep. We’ve run the same analysis on what Dogecoin (CRYPTO: DOGE) did after every 90% drop. So what does Cardano’s price history show about its performance six, 12, and 24 months after each major decline?
Cardano Has Hit Five Floors 90% Below a Prior High Since 2018

All five earlier lows led to gains after 12 months, even though ADA saw only a modest 16.0% gain following the December 2018 low. However, ADA broke two of these lows below, once in March 2020 after the December 2018 floor, and again in September 2023 after the December 2022 low.
The worst result came after the August 2024 low, with ADA trading 29.4% below that level by August 2026. That drop shapes how we assess Cardano’s potential recovery in 2027.
Staking, Smart Contracts and Politics Drove Each Cardano Rebound
The 2019 rebound had little behind it. ADA peaked at 10.71 cents in June 2019 but fell to a monthly close of 6.01 cents by July, continuing to decline until the pandemic sell-off in March 2020.
The price recovery in 2020, however, was driven by upgrades to the Cardano network. The Shelley upgrade allowed holders to stake ADA, securing the network while earning rewards. ADA then set its all-time high after Cardano announced the Alonzo hard fork, which brought smart contracts to the platform.
Later recoveries leaned on broader crypto rallies. In December 2023, ADA hit 67.7 cents, followed by a peak of $1.15 in November 2024 as Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) reached an all-time high after Trump’s election victory. In March 2025, ADA reached $1.19 after Trump named Cardano among the coins for a U.S. strategic crypto reserve. It last traded above $1 in August 2025, and our comparison of Cardano and XRP under $1 favors a return to that level.
While upgrades have boosted prices before, newer upgrades haven’t had the same effect as Alonzo. After Cardano completed its Van Rossum hard fork on July 18, 2026, ADA peaked at 26.52 cents in September 2026 but has since lost 42% of that value.
Cardano’s History Points to a Bounce, Not a Full Recovery
Based on Cardano’s history, a bounce from these deep lows looks likely, but a full recovery isn’t guaranteed. After each past floor, ADA gained within a year. However, its highest price after the 2021 peak was $1.32 in December 2024, which is still 757% above the current price. The long-term gain of 456.2% mainly reflects early investors and says little about those who bought near $3.10.
The next test will be Cardano’s Dijkstra upgrade, whose first phase targets code completion in the fourth quarter of 2026, according to Cardano.org. If ADA holds above its 13.32-cent low into 2027, history suggests a bounce like those in 2019 and 2023 might follow, as our look at $1,000 in Cardano by 2028 explores. But if ADA drops further, the 2018 and 2022 floors show the first deep low isn’t always the final bottom.

The year saw the UK experience its warmest summer on record, with parts of the country enduring multiple heatwaves over several months, beginning in late May when temperatures peaked at 35.1C at Kew Gardens in London, an all-time high for the month.
The heatwave at the end of June prompted a rare red alert from the Met Office for extreme heat and saw temperatures reach 38.0C on June 26 in Lingwood in Norfolk, another new monthly record.
As the scorching summer continued, England saw its driest July since data began, with only 7mm of rain measured, or 10 per cent of the long-term average.
The heatwave in mid-August saw temperatures climb as high as 38.2C at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire, making it the hottest day of the year.
The latest UKHSA report, which covers the period from late May to late August, adds that the “analysis is based on provisional mortality data and the final number will be published in the annual official statistics report in early 2027”.
UKHSA observed summer 2026 saw “an unusually high number of heat episodes, several periods of sustained hot weather” and noted that “more people living with health conditions sensitive to heat, increasing the number of people potentially vulnerable to the health effects of extreme heat”.
The highest number of heat-associated deaths were recorded between 21 and 28 June, when an estimated 2,401 deaths were linked to this period of extreme heat.
This year’s total of 5,258 deaths follows a run of much lower annual totals, with 2,295 in 2023, 1,311 in 2024 and 1,504 in 2025.
The report said intense heat early in the summer season “can pose particular risks as unusually hot weather may occur before people, communities and services have fully prepared and are ready to respond to hot weather conditions”.
It added: “These findings therefore reinforce the importance of heat-health preparedness measures being in place from the start of the season, rather than focusing solely on the warmest periods of mid-summer.”
Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental health scientist at the UKHSA, said: “Heat can affect anyone, but older adults, young children, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions are at greater risk.
“Climate change is already affecting people’s health in England, and as the climate continues to warm we can expect periods of extreme heat to become longer, more frequent and more intense.
“That is why it is vital that individuals, communities, health and care services and local organisations are prepared, not just during a heatwave but in the longer term.
“The decisions we make now will shape the health impacts people experience in the decades ahead.”
